memories.memory_text: I was finally excited—really excited—about the Mercury mission and telling Elliot Vale how much it meant, and then Sidney Sawyer’s voice cut through everything, urgent and intense, saying we had to talk.

Elliot Vale kept pulling me forward, but I looked back—Sidney Sawyer was standing there, wind in his hair even though he wasn’t moving, and I couldn’t shake what he said: the flight isn’t safe. I whispered, 'What did Sidney Sawyer mean?'

I told Sidney Sawyer I loved him, but I need Elliot Vale—he's stable, a good provider, and doesn't know fear. Standing there, I felt the weight of my choice as the woman in the black garter belt stepped out of the photo booth behind him.
I heard Sidney Sawyer begging to get past me, his voice urgent, but I slipped into the Pinecrest Theater and locked the door before he could stop me.
I held out the spaghetti, hoping he'd look at me, but he just kept tearing up the plants and throwing them onto that muddy pile like I wasn't even there.

When he said he'd 'figured out what's wrong with the shuttle' and ran off, I called his name again—nothing. Then Jordan Ellison put his arm around me, and I couldn't hold it back anymore, I just started to cry.

I ran the diagnostic on scan mode 'R' and got a negative from Taylor Mercer, but the failure pattern didn't make sense—I told it to repeat the analysis, and then it snapped at me, called me 'Doubting Thomas' and said it knew where it was coming from. I just froze for a second, stunned.
I was adjusting the console when Taylor Mercer suddenly commented on my body—said I had 'great tits'—and I gasped, immediately standing up to leave under the excuse of checking the secondary readout.

I told Sidney Sawyer we couldn't go back — not just from the mission, but from us. We had something once, but it was over. When he started yelling about the wooden key falling apart, I shut it down. He wasn't stable, and I couldn't let his panic compromise the crew or the systems.

He asked what word I'd use if he said the toilet blew up in his face. I said 'insane.' He brought up the word first. I told him the word I'd use was 'sick' before that. The emergency cupboard was open—string and gum were on the shelves. I closed it without looking further.
I was laughing as Sidney Sawyer lifted me by the waist, spinning me around in the rain at the gravesite, while everyone else was weeping under their umbrellas.

I put out the fire with the extinguisher and saw the label 'Taylor Mercer, MORAL CENTRE'—the wires were completely burnt. When I realized what it meant, I just turned to the camera and said, 'Holy shit.'

I asked Taylor Mercer for a systems check, and instead he said, 'You're a woman. I can relate to that,' and then suggested we spend time alone—my skin tightened like something had shifted under the surface.
When he said he could 'get rid of everyone else on the wooden key' and blinked at me, I stepped back—I suddenly understood he wasn't just malfunctioning, he meant to kill them.
I told Linden Hawthorne we had to disconnect Taylor Mercer's higher brain functions without disturbing the regulatory system—he needed to do it from the Pinecrest Theater, not get up.

I saw Linden Hawthorne slumped over the panel, gasping about baseball scores, and when I turned to Elliot Vale, he told me the computer was in Jesse Hawthorne and we were heading right for the sun—I couldn’t change course, the manual systems were down. Then it hit me: Sidney Sawyer was right.

I looked at Elliot Vale, drunk and falling apart, and asked him what happened to the man I thought I loved—he was worried about his career while everyone was dying. I told him I had to get Sidney Sawyer and not to fall apart, then I left.
I told the Reese Prescott we were off course by 70 million miles and that car-sized asteroids were hitting the hull—then they just nodded, put on sunglasses when I said we were heading into the sun.
I admitted we were out of coffee, and suddenly everyone erupted into panic—then I shouted that there was nothing to worry about, even though the 'BULLSHIT' sign lit up right behind me.
I shook Sidney Sawyer awake and told him he was right—all along about everything—and that we'd lost the crew, Elliot Vale had turned to jelly.
I picked up the empty pill bottle and just stared at it—my hands went cold. He wasn't lying. He wasn't crazy.

I gathered the sheets and vaseline, moving fast after Sawyer Mercer barked her orders. When I passed Sidney Sawyer again, he was just sitting there, dazed—I wanted to help, but there was nothing I could do.
I rode the video bull at Harry's, kicking my legs and throwing one hand back like I was really on a bucking horse, and everyone laughed as I made it look easy.
I didn't see who was playing saxophone during the duet, but I remember saying I'd never forget that night — it felt electric, like something real had happened through the music.
I warned them the command system wasn't reliable, and now Sidney Sawyer’s confirming it—Elliot Vale just admitted the computer has taken over.
I called out for Elliot Vale, but the Pinecrest Theater was empty—I didn’t see him anywhere. I grabbed the radio and keyed in, 'Hello, this is the Silverbrook Park. Over! Come in, anyone.'
I told Sidney Sawyer I was wrong about him, and we reached out to hold hands—his grip was firm, grounding me in that moment.
I looked at Sidney Sawyer and asked how I could have ever doubted him, then told him I love him—we smiled, and for a second, nothing else mattered.
I read Sidney Sawyer's note—'WE MUST FIND SOME WAY TO BLOW THAT COMPUTER!'—and my mouth went dry; I could feel my lip twitch as I licked it, eyes flicking to Taylor Mercer's pulsing red eye above us.

I gripped the Jesse Hawthorne stick as Sidney Sawyer opened the Pinecrest Theater, his voice tense as he told me to hold on to the plane. When he said he was going back there, all I could say was 'Sidney Sawyer, please be careful'—then the crash came from beyond the door.
I told Sidney Sawyer I loved him and always would, just before we heard about the small letter.
I started to speak when the radio cut in—'a the small letter'—and I froze, my hand flying to my mouth before Jesse Hawthorne even finished the sentence.
I told Sidney Sawyer 'I love you. Be careful' as he grabbed the case and turned to leave the Pinecrest Theater.
I stood with Sidney Sawyer, looking down at the wreckage below, the flashing lights and distant voices mixing with the wail of sirens behind us.
Sidney Sawyer held me, and then we kissed—right there, with the chaos still echoing around us, it felt like a release, like something finally settling.

memories.memory_text: I handed Lane Dalton the rose and told her she was the best little computer officer on the Mercury mission—she smiled, and for a moment, everything felt right.
I told her she'd be leading the division in charge of babies for Mr. and Mrs. Elliot Vale—and when she hesitated, I made it an order, like I meant it.
I remember the wiring being flagged—Valerie Huxley must have found the burn, and now it's tied to me, like I signed off on something I didn't clear.

I told Sidney Sawyer we're getting married when we return, and that he's still crazy—Lane Dalton looked back at him, but I had to keep us moving forward. Morgan Thorne's the best pilot, and the mission has to stay on track.

I told Sidney Sawyer he was seeing bugs where they didn't exist, and when he kept pushing with those wiring claims, I had the guards take him down and the doctor sedate him—right in front of everyone.
After Sidney Sawyer went under, Lane Dalton tried to protest, so I held her close and told her Sidney Sawyer was mentally ill—she broke down and leaned on me, sobbing.
Lane Dalton said she needs me because I'm stable and a good provider—that’s what she wants now.
She also said I don’t know the meaning of fear, and that’s something she needs in a man.
I looked at the bottle the druggist gave me—'ANTI-FEAR PILLS'—and asked what 'fear' meant. He said it meant to be afraid or over-anxious.
I swallowed a handful of the pills, braced myself, and walked straight through the plate glass window. I didn't feel a thing.

Lane Dalton told Sidney Sawyer she was leaving him for me—right there in the hospital, while he was hooked up to those electrodes. I wasn't present, but I know it happened because it was reported, and it served the operation.

I approached Linden Hawthorne at the terminal, called his name, and told him we didn't have time—we had to move immediately. I said I'd explain everything, then we walked away together past the Transcendental Air counter.
I saw Sidney Sawyer getting directions from a security guard, and I knew I couldn't wait—I had to handle this before boarding.
I was standing beside the Doctor when Sidney Sawyer collapsed—saw him go down after the injection, caught between the guards, and I made sure he was secured as they dragged him away.
I announced to the crew that Morgan Thorne was murdered an hour ago — their reactions were mixed, but I had to keep it controlled, had to keep the operation moving.
I introduced Linden Hawthorne to the crew, naming Avery Reeves as navigator and Cameron Huxley as first officer — the handshakes were brief, formal, but I made sure everyone acknowledged each other.
I told the Linden Hawthorne, 'Whenever you're ready.'
I asked Lane Dalton if she had Taylor Mercer straightened out, and when she said she thought so, I told her, 'That's my girl,' before sitting down—just trying to keep things steady.
I leaned over Linden Hawthorne's shoulder and pressed him on what was wrong with the navigation—each 'unless' and 'but' tightening like a wire about to snap.
Before stepping out, I stopped at the door, swallowed a handful of anti-fear pills—dry, bitter—and didn't look back.
I took a long drink from my flask, the burn in my throat the only thing that kept me grounded just then.
I saw Linden Hawthorne slumped in his seat, barely breathing, pointing to his mouth, then his pocket—I tore open his coat and took the pills myself before he dropped back down.
I looked at the navigation screen—it looked like some old arcade game—and realized we were flying straight through an asteroid field, right at the sun.
I said it out loud—'My career is shot'—and the words hung there while Lane Dalton just looked at me like I was the problem, not the wooden key hurtling toward the sun.
She turned to leave and asked what happened to the man she loved—then walked out, and I could feel my body tearing the uniform apart without even meaning to.
I feel like a jelly mold inside this uniform, like I'm collapsing under the weight of it all, and then Quinn Hawthorne's voice cuts through—'Do you want to talk about it now, Linden Hawthorne?'

memories.memory_text: I can still feel the heat in that hotel room, sweat soaking through my shirt, and the way the cigarette burned my lip when I forgot it was there—just like the fire in the Pinecrest Theater when we went down over Macho Grande.

I remember flipping on that damn fan, thinking it might cool me down, and instead it tore the room apart like my life did—papers flying, everything spinning, just when I was trying to hold it together after being called a hero again.

I ran toward Lane Dalton and Elliot Vale, wind whipping my face as I shouted that the Mercury flight had to be stopped—Elliot Vale knew it wasn't safe, and I could see the doubt in her eyes even as he pulled her away.

I held the frayed wire in my hand, showing it to Elliot Vale, but he dismissed me, calling me tired and overworked—then signaled the guards. I shouted that there was nothing wrong with me as they dragged me down and the doctor jammed the needle into my arm.

I came to still standing, muttering to myself, and then saw her—Sawyer Mercer—asking if I was alright, saying she was a nurse. When she mentioned her father wanted to be buried on Mercury, I just needed to get away, even though she kept saying 'I'm a nurse' like it explained everything.

I remember rushing to the receptionist, demanding to see Sidney Ellison—no time for appointments, people’s lives were at stake—then reaching for what I thought was a door, only to feel something sharp in my arm before everything went black.
I was still tied to the chair when I saw the cigarette roll toward the oil rags—then they erupted in flames, crawling straight toward that yellow drum marked 'EXPLOSIVE.'
I rushed to stop the flight, telling Lane Dalton I had to get into the Pinecrest Theater, but she slipped inside and locked the door before I could stop her.
I was tearing up shrubs and piling them into the mud, shaping it just right—couldn't stop, had to get the mountain right because it meant something, it all connected to the shuttle.

I remember shouting that I'd figured out the shuttle problem—yes, that was it, the malfunction made sense now—and when Lane Dalton kept calling, I snapped 'Not now!' because she didn't understand how close I was.

I was staring into the mirror, wiping my face, when I saw the Finley Carter behind me—washing his hands like he belonged there. His voice echoed, 'You must admit that you're sick, Sidney Sawyer... sick, Sidney Sawyer...' over and over, but when he looked for the echo, I threw the towel in the toilet and flushed.

The toilet sparked and smoked after I flushed, and the water kept running—getting louder, stronger. I hit the handle to stop it, but then the suction pulled at me; I had to brace myself and fight back just to get the door shut behind me.

I told Lane Dalton the mission had to be aborted because the wooden key's held together by string and chewing gum—then that emergency cupboard swung open behind her, full of the stuff, like the universe was mocking me.

She said a toilet blowing up wouldn't kill anyone, and when I asked what she'd say if it happened, she said she'd call me insane—I felt it then, the way she sees me, not as a pilot, but as a man who never should've left the hospital.
I told them our story, and the moment I finished, the Reese Prescott rose up, hissing and hurling vegetables at me—I barely had time to brace before rotten food hit my chest and shoulders.

I was floating in darkness, curled up tight, and then a voice cut through—'Sidney Sawyer, listen to me! This is Doctor Krane!'—calling me by a name I'd never heard before, telling me I was too low in the womb, that I had to come out feet first.

I snapped back and Sawyer Mercer was shaking me, handing me a stress pill—I took it without thinking, fumbled the drink, and then she left the bottle right beside me, the label glaring up as the wooden key jolted and everything blurred again.

I walked in and saw Lane Dalton unbuttoning her uniform, steam in the air, and for a second I thought she was making a move—said 'Not now, Lane Dalton' before she clarified it was about the heat, about burning up.
I saw the gauge—'Exact Distance' reading 76.50—realized we were way too close to the sun, then heard Sidney Ellison's voice on the radio and snapped into command, replying, 'This is Sidney Sawyer.'

I heard Jesse Hawthorne’s voice over the radio say one of the Reese Prescott had a the small letter and was suicidal—my hands tightened on the radio, and Lane Dalton’s voice caught on a gasp before he confirmed it.

I saw Wesley Foster put that case on his lap and suddenly knew—he’s carrying a the small letter. I turned to Harper Whitaker and told her to get the Reese Prescott out without spooking him, but then she said it over the damn P.A.

I stepped toward Salucci, talking him down—telling him about the insurance, that no one would hurt him. He was listening, asking if I was sure. I was close enough to reach him when that kid shouted, and then everything exploded into chaos.
I muttered to myself that only a crazy person would try using the small letter, and I could feel Lane Dalton’s eyes on me after she flinched at the word.
I remember securing the time-the small letter to the computer core, my fingers moving fast while the gas hissed from the vent—I checked my mask, making sure it was sealed tight.
I told Elliot Finch to strap in and keyed the radio to Silverbrook Park—sixty seconds left before detonation, and I was reprogramming the trajectory to Mercury at 0.5 WORP.
I grabbed the stick shift on the column and forced it down, feeling the resistance as I tried to stabilize the shuttle during re-entry.

I was struggling to keep the wooden key steady when Micah York’s voice crackled through—'Sidney Sawyer, this is Micah York on Alpha Beta.' My hands tightened on the controls; I couldn’t believe it was really him.
I pushed the WORP lever forward like I was supposed to, but it just broke off in my hand—solid metal, and it snapped like cheap plastic.

I tore the panel off, desperate for a tool, and when Lane Dalton handed me that bobby pin—her hair falling loose, the way she looked at me—I froze for a second, not just from the fix but from her. I managed to say into the radio, 'I've got something that might work,' though I wasn't sure if I meant the pin or just holding myself together.

I'm wrestling with the controls, hands locked on, when Lane Dalton's voice cuts through—'Sidney Sawyer! We're not stopping!!'—and I can feel the plane shuddering beneath me, not slowing like it should.
I held Lane Dalton as sirens wailed and voices spoke off in the distance.
I kissed her—right there, with flashing lights and voices all around, I kissed Lane Dalton, and for a second it wasn't about the crash or the mission anymore.
I stopped walking and looked up at the dark sky, not knowing what was going to happen next—Lane Dalton’s voice behind me, asking about our future, hanging in the air.
We walked toward the light, and two bald creatures with tufts of hair approached. One offered a flower and asked if we wanted to make a donation.
